newsitem.title: INDIA: India's Congress closes ranks for Gandhi apostle.
newsitem.headline: India's Congress closes ranks for Gandhi apostle.

text.p: India's sickly Congress party has tapped a disciple of Mahatma Gandhi as stop-gap chief, but a fierce struggle now looms as the nation's oldest party looks for a leader to take it into the 21st century.

The party's top decision-making body reached into the past to choose Sitaram Kesri, 80, a former freedom fighter during the independence movement, as interim leader on Monday to replace former prime minister P.V. Narasimha Rao.
Rao quit abruptly on Saturday after a judge ordered him to appear him in court in a $100,000 criminal conspiracy case.

Kesri, who has served as Congress treasurer for 18 years, drew broad but not unequivocal support to take over the reins until the fractious party's plenary body meets to select a more permanent leader.

The date of that meeting has not been set, but it was agreed that the party should await the outcome of assembly elections in India's most populous state Uttar Pradesh, which start next Monday and end on October 7.
Kesri boasted the advantage of having links to Congress's heyday when it dominated the political stage. He also commands the confidence of Rao and his loyalists.
Asked what his first priority would be, Kesri said he would "carry on the message of Mahatma Gandhi to wipe out tears from the eyes of the downtrodden, the poor and the oppressed."
On Tuesday, Kesri said he would focus on healing Congress's deep divisions. "I will leave no stone unturned to bring about Congress unity," the Press Trust of India quoted him as saying.
As a low-caste Hindu, Kesri stands out within an organisation that has traditionally been led by the Brahmin elite.
He takes over just before elections in Uttar Pradesh, where Congress is pinning its hopes on an unprecedented alliance with a low-caste regional party.

Congress, intended since its creation in 1885 as an over-arching organisation with a national reach, has seen its influence wane in recent years as new parties reflecting caste and regional interests sprouted.
Kesri was described by The Pioneer newspaper as "a drawing room political fund raiser," reflecting his power as a party insider without an electoral base.
The octogenarian with a history of heart trouble was only expected to tide over the party until a more permanent successor is chosen.
Rival contenders were expected to put up a fierce fight.
The Hindustan Times said Congress had reached an "uneasy consensus" in tapping Kesri as a compromise candidate.
The Press Trust of India said that a "visibly agitated Rajesh Pilot," who was environment minister under Rao, had pointedly noted that the choice of Kesri was not unanimous.
Pilot, 51, a member of Congress who is widely known to be interested in the leadership post, left "his stamp of dissent" at the meeting, The Asian Age said.
"This is his (Pilot's) style of functioning," Kesri said on Tuesday. "I am pained that Mr Pilot stood isloated in yesterday's meeting."
